# Mexican-period sawmilling and lumber shipping on Richardson Bay / Tiburon peninsula (1830s-1846)

## 1. John Thomas Reed (Juan Read) and his sawmill

### The grant (primary: federal court record, quoted in full)
Hoffman's *Reports of Land Cases* (1862), as quoted verbatim in Munro-Fraser (1880), p. 189, for *The United States v. The Heirs of Juan Read* (Rancho Corte de Madera del Presidio, Land Case 183 ND): the land was **granted to Juan Read by Governor Figueroa on October 2, 1834**; the territorial deputation approved the concession October 2, 1835; **judicial possession was given November 28, 1835**; Read "resided with his family on the land" until his death, and the court called it "one of the few instances where every requirement of the law has been fully complied with." [PRIMARY: court report] Bancroft's Pioneer Register agrees: Read was "naturalized in Sept. '34, and in Oct. was grantee of the Corte de Madera del Presidio rancho" (Bancroft, *History of California*, V, Pioneer Register, s.v. "Read (John)"; grant also listed at III, 711). The grant was patented to Reed's heirs in 1885 for 7,845 acres, covering southern Corte Madera, Mill Valley, Strawberry Point and the Tiburon peninsula (Wikipedia, *Rancho Corte Madera del Presidio*, tertiary; patent date is standard). Note Munro-Fraser's township chapter (p. 385) alternatively says Reed "in 1833, applied for and received a grant" and that "the final papers of this grant were made out in 1843"; the dated court record (Oct. 2, 1834) is to be preferred.

### Reed's career (Bancroft, Pioneer Register, V, s.v. "Read (John)") [secondary, closest to the archival record]
Irish sailor, "said to have come from Acapulco" in 1826, though Bancroft found "no original record of his presence before '33 except that in '34 several witnesses testified to having known him for 6 years, or since '28." Refused the Saucelito grant (Munro-Fraser p. 110: applied 1826, refused because the land "was held for Government purposes"); driven off the Cotate rancho by Indians; majordomo of Mission San Rafael; settled at Saucelito in 1832 (Weeks claimed to have visited his cabin there in 1831); "his boat running occasionally to Yerba Buena, may be regarded as the 1st ferry" on the bay. Married Hilaria Sanchez 1836; administrator of San Rafael; visited by Edwards 1837 and by Henry A. Peirce 1841; **died in 1843** (Munro-Fraser p. 111: of a botched bleeding during a fever, aged 38, buried at San Rafael). Bancroft's register entry says nothing about a sawmill.

### The mill: what the sources actually say about its date
The sources genuinely conflict, and the user's "1834/1836" question has no clean answer:
- **Munro-Fraser 1880, general chapter (p. 110):** after the 1834 grant "he erected a saw mill, the first in the county" (undated).
- **Munro-Fraser 1880, Saucelito township chapter, "Mills" (pp. 388-389):** "He erected his saw-mill **in 1843**, and had but just got it in operation when he died. His prime object in building it was to saw lumber for his house, which he had in process of construction when he died." This chapter is internally damaged (it also puts Reed's death in 1848, against p. 111 and Bancroft's 1843), but its mill description is the most detailed on record: "It was a **sash-saw** and was **driven by water-power**, and while its capacity was not very great, it was far superior to whip-sawing, which was the usual mode of making lumber at that time. It was located in the ravine about one-half mile south-west of the Read ranch house... it evidently worked up a great amount of timber. Only a few posts and slabs are left to mark the site" (1880).
- **California Historical Landmark No. 207** ("First Sawmill in Marin County," registered June 20, 1935): "This mill was erected by John Reed **about 1833-34**." [landmark tradition]
- **Mill Valley Historic Resources Inventory (adopted June 7, 2021), fn. 7:** "the original mill was constructed by John Reed in **circa 1834**."
- **Marin IJ (Jan. 2025):** "erected **around 1835**." Local tradition (e.g. Reed Heights POA history) also circulates **1836**.
- Contemporary silence: Bancroft's note on Edwards's 1837 trip names "Cooper's Mill" (Sonoma) by name but only "Read's rancho" (IV, p. 86 n. 14); W. H. Davis (*Sixty Years in California*, 1889, p. 281), describing the pre-1843 trade, says bay-area lumber came from runaway-sailor whip-sawyers "there being no saw-mills in the department" (loose recollection, but notable). Davis dates the first steam sawmill on the coast to Stephen Smith's Bodega mill, landed 1843 (pp. 149-150).
**Bottom line:** c. 1834 is the canonical (landmark) date and cannot be disproven; the only detailed 19th-century account says 1843; no contemporary Mexican-period document dating the mill was found in this pass. A map label of "c. 1834-1843 (date disputed)" is the defensible form.

### What it cut and for whom
Munro-Fraser (pp. 385-386, 388): the mill's "prime object" was lumber for Reed's own two-story adobe; "the timber and lumber used in the construction of this house was sawed at the mill on the Read ranch." The Mill Valley Historical Society (2015) corroborates: "The wood for the beams and the veranda was cut at Reed's Mill in Cascade Canyon." The often-repeated claim that the mill "cut wood for the Presidio" rests on the landmark tradition and on the rancho's NAME, which predates the mill: Munro-Fraser p. 385 explains the rancho "derived its name from the fact that the timbers and lumber for the erection of the presidio buildings at Yerba Buena had been brought from this place," i.e. the pre-grant woodcutting trade, not the mill's output. Reed also ran a separate **horse-powered grist mill**, its basalt stones "purchased from the Russians at Fort Ross" (Munro-Fraser p. 388; the stones survive and were dedicated at the Outdoor Art Club per an MVHS event notice).

### How lumber moved
**No Mexican-period source found documents how (or whether) Reed's sawn lumber moved off the rancho**; no embarcadero, cart road or boat landing for the mill is attested in anything consulted (Munro-Fraser, Bancroft, Toogood, MVHS, diseños). Both diseños of the rancho examined (Bancroft Land Case Maps, digicoll recs 78639 and 79070) show "Casa de Dn. Juan Read," the Presidio, Sausalito anchorage and bay soundings, but **no molino and no landing**. The documented water movement of timber on Richardson Bay is American-period: in 1849 "a great amount of timber and piling was cut here and taken across the bay" and the Parker-Botts-McCormack government steam mill at old Saucelito (Nov. 1849-1852) had its logs cut "near the head of Richardson's bay... rafted around to the mill" (Munro-Fraser pp. 388-389).

### The mill's later fate
By 1880 "only a few posts and slabs" marked the site (Munro-Fraser p. 389). **Old Mill Park was given to the city by the Tamalpais Land & Water Company in 1900**; CHL No. 207 registered **June 20, 1935**; "the mill structure was **reconstructed according to historic photographs, physical evidence and other sources in 1991**" (Mill Valley HRI 2021, fn. 7, citing "Reed's Mill: The Story of the Old Mill and of its reconstruction in 1991," *Mill Valley Historical Review*, 1992). Marin IJ (Jan. 2025) confirms "a major rebuild in 1991" and a pending roof rehabilitation with redwood shakes. The standing structure is a **replica** (MVHS 2015: "A replica of the original mill is on the creek at Old Mill Park today"). Note: a "1930s restoration" is NOT supported; 1935 was the landmark designation, 1991 the reconstruction. Also note the CHL 207 **plaque stands away from the mill**, at Blithedale Ave and Tower Dr (37.90379, -122.51918 per californiahistoricallandmarks.com); do not map the plaque as the mill.

## 2. William A. Richardson and Sausalito

Bancroft's Pioneer Register (V, p. 694-695) is the anchor: arrived 1822 (mate of the whaler *Orion*), permitted to stay by Sola on condition of teaching navigation and carpentry; naturalized 1830; erected the first dwelling of Yerba Buena 1835; **captain of the port from January 1, 1837** (Munro-Fraser p. 111 says appointed June 1835); "**His private business was the collection of country produce by a launch running on the bay**"; "in '36 he became owner of the Sauzalito rancho, granted to Galindo in '35; and in '41 he went there to live," with "no little trouble arising from his interested leniency to whalers who insisted on going to Sauzalito 'for wood and water.'" Munro-Fraser (p. 111) instead dates the Saucelito grant February 11, 1838 and his removal there April 1836; Toogood (NPS, 1980, p. 52 n. 34, citing Kinnaird and Mason) has the grant "officially in 1838 by Governor Alvarado and made final on February 11, 1839," removal 1838-39 (a note in Dwinelle's 1840 list of foreigners: Richardson "having for some time been at Sausalito"). Bancroft explicitly brands the Munro-Fraser Richardson sketch "very inaccurate" (register entry); Bancroft has him dying in 1856 (modern consensus; Munro-Fraser's April 22, 1858 is wrong).

**Sausalito as Whalers' Harbor (Puerto de los Balleneros):** whalers and traders preferred to anchor at Sauzalito for "the greater conveniences... for obtaining wood and water; but the chief motive was a desire to be free from all legal restraints," Richardson siding with the whalers (Bancroft IV, pp. 429-430); the Russian-American Co. (Kostromitinov) obtained Richardson's consent to build a warehouse at "Puerto de Balleneros" in 1835-36 before the diputacion vetoed it (Bancroft IV, 163-164); the Wilkes expedition ships lay 80 days at Sausalito in 1841, Richardson "very attentive and obliging in furnishing the ship with supplies" (Toogood pp. 54-55, quoting Wilkes; standard authority: Boyd Huff, *El Puerto de los Balleneros: Annals of the Sausalito Whaling Anchorage*, 1957). Richardson arranged "to sell them water and other provisions" (Toogood p. 53), his rancho's "thousands of cattle, horses, and sheep... helped furnish provisions for ships anchoring at Sausalito Cove" (Davis via Toogood).

**Lumber:** NO source consulted shows Richardson milling or shipping LUMBER in the Mexican period. The "wood" whalers took at Whalers' Harbor was firewood-and-water provisioning, not a lumber trade. His documented freight (Soule's *Annals* via Toogood p. 53 n. 35) was hides (12 cents each), tallow ($1/bag) and grain (25 cents/fanega) carried in his Indian-crewed launches. No source seen documents a Richardson wharf of the 1850s either; the American-period lumber facilities at old Saucelito on record are the 1849-52 government steam mill and the government stores (Munro-Fraser pp. 387-389).

## 3. Context: the 'corte de madera' woodcutting economy

The redwood canyons at the head of Richardson Bay were a named woodcutting ground before any mill existed: the 1828 register of Mission San Rafael's lands already locates the "rancheria of Annamus, called San Pedro Alcantara, **in the Corte de Madera**, and the Rinconada del Tiburon" (Bancroft II, 597-598 n., from the MS *Register of Brands*), and Munro-Fraser (p. 385) explains the rancho name, "the place where wood is cut for the Presidio," by the fact "that the timbers and lumber for the erection of the presidio buildings at Yerba Buena had been brought from this place." Through the Mexican period the standard production method around the bay was whip-sawing by itinerant sailor-sawyers (Davis, *Sixty Years*, p. 281; Munro-Fraser p. 389 contrasts Reed's sash-saw with "whip-sawing, which was the usual mode of making lumber at that time"), and Sauzalito's role was as the wood-and-water anchorage (Bancroft IV, 429-430). Commercial lumber EXPORT from the Richardson Bay / Corte Madera redwoods is a Gold Rush phenomenon: the 1849 timber-and-piling trade across the bay, the government steam mill at old Saucelito rafting logs from the head of Richardson's Bay (Munro-Fraser pp. 388-389), and the Baltimore & Frederick company's 1849 steam mill with its creek-bank wharves on tidal Corte Madera Creek (already in the project dataset as "Corte Madera Creek landings"). An "old government saw-mill" on a tributary of Corte Madera Creek appears as a landmark in the 1862 township boundaries (Munro-Fraser p. 200); it is unidentified in this pass and is presumably American-period.

## What is NOT supported (explicit)
1. **No "Tiburon mill" exists in the record.** No source shows any Mexican-period mill on the Tiburon peninsula proper. The mill the user is after is Reed's, at today's Old Mill Park, Mill Valley, on Old Mill Creek (Arroyo Corte Madera del Presidio watershed), which drains to Richardson Bay. The Tiburon connection is simply that the peninsula lay within Reed's rancho. The phrase "the Tiburon or Richardson Bay mill" should resolve on the map to "Reed's sawmill (Mill Valley)."
2. **No embarcadero or lumber-shipping point for Reed's mill is documented** for the Mexican period; do not map one.
3. **No Richardson lumber operation** (milling or shipping) in the Mexican period; his Sausalito anchorage was a provisioning point (wood/water/beef) and his launches carried hides, tallow and produce. A Richardson-built 1850s wharf was not found in the sources consulted.
4. **A 1930s restoration of the mill is not supported**: 1935 = CHL designation; the reconstruction is 1991.
5. The claim that the mill itself "cut wood for the Presidio" is landmark tradition; the period evidence ties the Presidio to the pre-grant woodcutting that named the rancho, and ties the mill's output to Reed's own buildings.
6. Munro-Fraser's two chapters disagree on the mill date (post-1834 vs. 1843) and on Reed's death year (1843 vs. 1848); 1843 death is certain (Bancroft, and p. 111).

features.coord_source: OSM building footprints straddling Old Mill Creek in Old Mill Park (ways 629380678-81, immediately upstream of the Old Mill Street end at Cascade Drive), cross-checked against the Old Mill Park polygon (OSM way 44421422, GNIS feature 1800530, centroid 37.90506,-122.55297) and Wikidata Q49535119 (37.905,-122.55306). features.coord_precision: building (~25-30 m); the ORIGINAL mill site is 'in the ravine' per Munro-Fraser 1880 and is conventionally identified with the replica's location
features.active_years: c. 1834-1843+ (construction date disputed: CHL 207 'about 1833-34'; local tradition 1836; Munro-Fraser township chapter says erected 1843, 'just got it in operation when he died'); ruins by 1880; park 1900; CHL designated 1935; replica reconstructed 1991
features.summary: First sawmill in Marin County: John T. Reed's water-powered sash-saw mill on Old Mill Creek, Rancho Corte Madera del Presidio, the mill that named Mill Valley. Its documented output was lumber and beams for Reed's own adobe buildings; superior to the whip-sawing that was 'the usual mode of making lumber at that time.' Not on the Tiburon peninsula: it sits at the head of the Richardson Bay watershed. The structure in Old Mill Park today is a 1991 reconstruction (CHL No. 207, registered 1935).
features.notes: Coords are [lat, lon]. Do NOT use the CHL 207 plaque location (Blithedale Ave & Tower Dr, 37.90379,-122.51918 per californiahistoricallandmarks.com); the plaque stands ~3 km east of the mill. Munro-Fraser places the mill 'about one-half mile south-west of the Read ranch house'; measured from the La Goma/Locke adobe site the replica is ~1 mi NW, so treat his bearing loosely. Separate horse-powered grist mill (Fort Ross basalt stones, surviving at the Outdoor Art Club) stood on the rancho, location unknown.

Russian warehouse project at 'Puerto de Balleneros' vetoed 1836. Wilkes's squadron lay here 80 days in 1841. No Mexican-period lumber milling or lumber shipping by Richardson is documented.

gaps: 1. Mill construction date: no contemporary Mexican-period document dating the mill was found. The decisive unexamined source is the transcript of Land Case 183 ND (U.S. v. Heirs of Juan Read, Bancroft Library): witness testimony there very likely mentions the mill and could settle 1834 vs 1836 vs 1843. Also unexamined: Henry A. Peirce's 1841 account of visiting Read's place (cited by Bancroft) and G. M. Waseurtz af Sandels's 1842-43 travel account. 2. 'Reed's Mill: The Story of the Old Mill and of its reconstruction in 1991' (Mill Valley Historical Review, 1992) is offline; the Lucretia Little History Room holds it; it would give the authoritative reconstruction narrative and probably MVHS's dating argument. 3. Jack Mason, Early Marin, and Barry Spitz, Mill Valley: The Early Years (1997), and the Tiburon history Shark Point - High Point (1958) are lending-restricted on IA; not read. 4. Mill coordinate is anchored on OSM footprints and the park polygon (~25-30 m); HMdb (Cloudflare) and the GNIS web app (SPA) blocked direct verification; a field-checked or city-GIS coordinate for the replica would tighten it. 5. The 'old government saw-mill' named in the 1862 township boundary near Corte Madera Creek (Munro-Fraser p. 200) is unidentified; presumably American-period; worth a targeted look (possible 1847 US quartermaster mill) since it could be confused with Reed's mill. 6. mvhistory.org and cityofmillvalley.gov content pages are bot-blocked; MVHS 'History of Early Mill Valley' page (which may state their preferred mill date, possibly 1836) could not be retrieved even via Wayback. 7. WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start; all discovery ran through curl/DuckDuckGo/Wayback/IA APIs, so coverage of recent journalism and Anne T. Kent California Room Medium articles on Reed is incomplete.
